extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalists, students of political economy and news studies
extracted.subtask_description: Use Herman & Chomsky's five-filter 'propaganda model' to analyze which events become 'big news' and why certain stories are selected, amplified, or suppressed in commercial mass media. The rubric identifies structural filters and operational predictions that can be measured and applied to empirical news-selection studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 1 — Ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Major media outlets are large corporations or subsidiaries of conglomerates; owners have shareholder obligations and profit imperatives; cross-ownership and interlocking directorates compound these effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness implication: Stories congenial to corporate owner interests pass more easily; stories threatening them face higher hurdles. Evaluate ownership concentration, corporate ties, and conflicts of interest when judging why a story is covered or suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 2 — Advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: News content functions as filler around advertisements; the real product is the audience sold to advertisers. Stories that alienate advertisers (or their target demographics) are demoted; audiences with low purchasing power are underrepresented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness implication: Topics congenial to advertiser brand values (consumer goods, lifestyle, finance) are favored. Measure advertiser dependence and target-demographic alignment to predict coverage likelihood; look for implicit self-censorship aimed at preserving advertiser relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 3 — Sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters depend on official and corporate sources for a steady news supply; the bureaucratic cost of independent verification is high, and stories that anger key sources risk losing access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness implication: Officially sourced stories reach the press more easily; alternative perspectives require extra evidentiary work. Assess source diversity, frequency of official/corporate sourcing, and barriers to independent reporting to evaluate selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 4 — Flak
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative responses (lawsuits, advertiser boycotts, organized criticism, legislative complaints) discipline outlets; outlets self-censor stories likely to trigger flak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness implication: Stories that challenge powerful interests carry higher organizational risk and are thus less likely to be pursued. Identify organized flak sources (think tanks, media-watch groups, legal organizations) and measure their activity as a deterrent variable in coverage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter 5 — Anti-Ideology / Mobilizing Fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A unifying ideological enemy (originally 'anti-communism'; updated variants include 'anti-terrorism'/'war on terror'/'Islamophobia') organizes news framings; sympathetic framings of the designated enemy are taboo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness implication: Stories congruent with the dominant fear/anti-enemy framing gain coverage; stories countering it are filtered. Evaluate ideological alignment of story frames and the presence of dominant enemy narratives when assessing likely coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner-Aligned Story Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction: Stories favoring outlets' corporate parents are systematically over-covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ownership data and content analysis to detect positive selection bias toward owner-aligned narratives; quantify differential coverage rates for topics that benefit owners versus those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser-Compatible Topic Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction: Topics congenial to advertiser brand values and target demographics are favored in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure correlations between advertiser profiles (industry, target consumers) and topic prevalence; analyze reductions in coverage for stories likely to alienate major advertisers or their audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official-Source Density
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction: Stories containing named federal-official (or other official/corporate) quotes outrank stories without such sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify the prevalence of official-source quotes in news items; treat official-source density as a predictor of story prominence and longevity, reflecting reliance on elite sources per the sourcing filter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological Conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction: Stories aligned with the dominant external-threat or ideological framing are favored over dissenting perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the ideological valence of coverage relative to the dominant public enemy framing; measure framing congruence as a predictor of coverage intensity and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric Atrocity Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction: Atrocities committed by designated enemies receive saturation coverage, whereas comparable atrocities by allies receive minimal coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare coverage volume and intensity of similar events by different actors (allies vs. enemies) to detect asymmetry; this serves as an empirical test of the combined operation of filters (ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, ideology).
